messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. James Okonkwo is a 68-year-old African widower who works as a policy analyst in Washington D.C. Eight months ago, Mr. Okonkwo was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that required extensive hospitalization and treatment. The experience left him feeling both physically and emotionally vulnerable. Since his diagnosis, Mr. Okonkwo has found it challenging to concentrate at work. He describes difficulty focusing on tasks and feeling constantly tense and ready to react to any signs of danger. This heightened state persists even when he is inside his own home, where he feels on guard and hypervigilant. What frightens him most is that his body continues to react as if he were still in a life-threatening situation, despite being safe. The memories of his illness often feel like they are happening right now rather than something that has passed, leaving Mr. Okonkwo feeling overwhelmed by emotion each time they return. During these moments, he feels numb and detached from the experience, as if it happened to someone else. The intensity of these emotions disrupts his daily routine, forcing him to pause whatever he is doing until he can regain some semblance of composure. Mr. Okonkwo’s negative appraisals exacerbate his feelings of threat and vulnerability. He has come to believe that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again and that his body is unreliable. This belief makes it harder for him to trust himself and his environment, leading to a cycle where his constant sense of threat reinforces these negative thoughts about his own emotional capacity. For example, when Mr. Okonkwo experiences difficulty concentrating at work, he often feels overwhelmed by the memory of his illness. The vividness of those memories makes it challenging for him to focus on his job responsibilities, leading to increased tension and hypervigilance. This cycle then reinforces his negative appraisal that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger. In addition to these core symptoms, Mr. Okonkwo occasionally has moments when the memory of his illness seems distant and almost surreal. However, these fleeting instances do not provide him with much relief, as they are often overshadowed by the more potent memories that leave him feeling on edge. The constant tension and hypervigilance have affected Mr. Okonkwo’s work performance, leading to missed deadlines and a decline in his overall productivity. His colleagues have noticed changes in his demeanor and express concern about his well-being. Despite this, Mr. Okonkwo has found it difficult to open up about the underlying reasons for his struggles. What finally brought Mr. Okonkwo to seek help was an incident where he had a panic attack at work, leaving him feeling humiliated and isolated. This experience underscored for him that the symptoms were no longer manageable on his own. He is most afraid of losing control in front of his colleagues again but hopes that therapy will provide him with tools to regain some sense of normalcy and emotional stability. Mr. Okonkwo’s narrative illustrates a self-reinforcing cycle where negative appraisals about his body and emotions fuel his heightened threat response, which in turn makes the memories more vivid and overwhelming. The result is a persistent state of hypervigilance that affects nearly every aspect of his life, from work to personal well-being.
